# Step 4: every robot finds the centroid (Lemma 3, Corollaries 2 and 3) {#sec-step4}

$L_\sigma$ needs every robot's $x_i = p_i - p_c$, and no robot knows the centroid. Section IV of the paper (all new with
respect to the conference version) computes it with a consensus estimator. **Lemma 3**: for quantities $y_i$ on a
connected graph, the estimator
$$
\dot{\hat y}_i = -\sum_{j\in\mathcal N_i}\Big[(\hat y_i - \hat y_j) - (y_i - y_j)\Big]
$$
keeps the average of the estimates constant and converges exponentially, at the rate of the algebraic connectivity
$\lambda_2(L)$ of the graph, to $\hat y_i = y_i - y_c + \hat y_c(0)$. Each robot only needs the *differences* $y_i - y_j$
with its neighbours and their estimates $\hat y_j$. **Corollary 2** applies it to the positions: the differences are the
measured $p_i - p_j = x_i - x_j$, and if every robot starts from $\hat x_i(0) = 0$, then $\hat x_i \to x_i$. Each robot then
knows where the centroid is, $p_i - \hat x_i$, in its own frame. (**Corollary 3**: start one robot from $-x_k$ instead,
and every robot learns its position relative to robot $k$.)

This is the formation controller turned around. In displacement-based formation control the robots move ($p_i$ changes)
until the measured $p_i - p_j$ match fixed desired values; here the robots' *software* values move until their
differences match the measured ones.

**The paper's ten-robot graph** (Figs. 4 and 5, eleven links) has $\lambda_2$ = `{python} f3(lam2_10)` (the published version says 0.26,
@sec-checks, item 6): the error shrinks by a factor of 100 in $\ln 100/\lambda_2$ = `{python} f1(t99)` time units. With ten
robots of this page in a box like the paper's, the largest error $\max_i\|\hat x_i - x_i\|$ is `{python} f2(err4[0])` at
the start, `{python} f3(err4[5])` at $t = 5$ and `{python} e2(err4[20])` at $t = 20$. The example's twenty robots have a
much denser graph, $\lambda_2$ = `{python} f2(lam2_1)`.

```{=html}

```

```{python}
#| echo: false
# ---------------------------------------------------------------- Step 5: the direction estimator (Cor. 4)
mu5 = [[sigma(F1, P1[i]) * X1[i][0], sigma(F1, P1[i]) * X1[i][1]] for i in range(N1)]
muc5 = centroid(mu5)
ratio5 = [muc5[0] / L1v[0], muc5[1] / L1v[1]]
run5 = estimator_run(mu5, E1, 0.001, 3000, every=100)
def dir_err(run_k):
    a = math.atan2(muc5[1], muc5[0])
    return max(abs(wrap(math.atan2(mu5[i][1] - run_k[i][1], mu5[i][0] - run_k[i][0]) - a)) for i in range(N1))
derr5 = [dir_err(r) for r in run5]
```

# Step 5: every robot finds the direction (Corollary 4) {#sec-step5}

The sum in $L_\sigma$ is an average: $L_\sigma = \mu_c / D^2$ with
$$
\mu_c = \frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N \mu_i, \qquad \mu_i = \sigma(p_i)\,x_i ,
$$
and only its direction matters, so neither $N$ nor $D$ is needed. Each robot computes its own $\mu_i$ from its reading and
its estimate of $x_i$. **Corollary 4** runs the same estimator on $y_i = \mu_i$: with $\hat\mu_i(0) = 0$,
$\hat\mu_i \to \mu_i - \mu_c$, so every robot can form $\mu^i_c = \mu_i - \hat\mu_i \to \mu_c$. Here the robots send their
neighbours both $\mu_j$ and $\hat\mu_j$. The cost is local: each robot works and talks in proportion to its number of
neighbours.

**In the example, at $t = 0$:** $\mu_c$ = (`{python} f4(muc5[0])`, `{python} f4(muc5[1])`), which is $D^2$ = `{python} f1(Dsz1**2)`
times $L_\sigma$ (the ratios are `{python} f2(ratio5[0])` and `{python} f2(ratio5[1])`). It is small: the robots' own
$\mu_i$ are up to `{python} f0(mu_ratio)` times larger, because the readings are all about the same and most of each
$\mu_i$ cancels in the average. So the estimates must shrink their error well below that factor before the direction
comes out right. With the robots held still and $\epsilon_\mu = 1$, the worst robot's direction $\mu^i_c$ is
`{python} deg(derr5[10])` off at $t = 1$, `{python} deg(derr5[20])` off at $t = 2$ and `{python} deg(derr5[30])` off at
$t = 3$. This is why the paper's simulations make this estimator fast, $\epsilon_\mu = 0.001$: a time unit of the estimator
is then a millisecond of the robots.

```{=html}
<div id="ex-mu" class="column-body"></div><script>EX.figs.wMu("ex-mu")</script>
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
# ---------------------------------------------------------------- Step 6: the closed loop (eq. 15, Theorem 1)
r1 = cached("sim1", lambda: paper_sim1(every=500))
r2 = cached("sim2", lambda: paper_sim2(every=500))
def stats(run, F):
    ps = source(F)
    T, dist, cerr, derr, alive = [], [], [], [], []
    for f in run:
        al = f["alive"]
        P = [q for q, a in zip(f["p"], al) if a]
        c = centroid(P)
        L = L_sigma(F, P)
        a = math.atan2(L[1], L[0])
        T.append(f["t"])
        dist.append(norm([c[0] - ps[0], c[1] - ps[1]]))
        cerr.append(max(norm([f["p"][i][0] - f["xh"][i][0] - c[0], f["p"][i][1] - f["xh"][i][1] - c[1]]) for i in range(len(al)) if al[i]))
        derr.append(max(abs(wrap(math.atan2(f["muc"][i][1], f["muc"][i][0]) - a)) for i in range(len(al)) if al[i]))
        alive.append(sum(al))
    return np.array(T), np.array(dist), np.array(cerr), np.array(derr), np.array(alive)
T1, dist1, cerr1, derr1, _ = stats(r1, F1)
reach1 = float(T1[np.argmax(dist1 < 5)])
appr1 = (T1 >= 1) & (T1 <= 15)
late1 = T1 >= reach1
```

# Step 6: the whole loop for robots that move like points (Theorem 1) {#sec-step6}

Each robot runs the two estimators and moves at speed $v$ along its own estimate of the direction, while a formation
controller holds the shape (equation (15), Fig. 1 of the paper):
$$
\begin{aligned}
\epsilon_x\,\dot{\hat x}_i &= -\textstyle\sum_{j\in\mathcal N_i}\big[(\hat x_i - \hat x_j) - (p_i - p_j)\big], \\
\epsilon_\mu\,\dot{\hat \mu}_i &= -\textstyle\sum_{j\in\mathcal N_i}\big[(\hat \mu_i - \hat \mu_j) - (\mu_i - \mu_j)\big],
\qquad \mu_i = \sigma(p_i)\,\hat x_i,\quad \mu^i_c = \mu_i - \hat\mu_i, \\
\dot p_i &= v\,\frac{\mu^i_c}{\|\mu^i_c\|} - k_f\textstyle\sum_{j\in\mathcal N_i}\big[(p_i - p_j) - (p^d_i - p^d_j)\big].
\end{aligned}
$$
The formation term does not move the centroid (its sum over the robots is zero), and a common velocity does not change
the shape, so the two tasks do not fight. **Theorem 1**: if the start is not degenerate, the condition of Proposition 2
holds on an annulus around the source, and the estimators are fast enough ($\epsilon_x < \epsilon_\mu$, both small), the
loop solves the problem. The proof stacks two singular perturbations (Khalil's Theorem 11.4): first the centroid
estimator, then the direction estimator, then the motion.

**In the example** ($v$ = `{python} D1["speed"]`, $k_f$ = `{python} D1["k_form"]`, $\epsilon_x$ = `{python} D1["ep_x"]`,
$\epsilon_\mu$ = `{python} D1["ep_mu"]`, Euler steps of $10^{-4}$, as in the paper's code). During the approach
($1 \le t \le 15$) every robot's centroid estimate is within `{python} f3(cerr1[appr1].max())` of the true centroid and
its direction within `{python} deg(derr1[appr1].max())` of $L_\sigma$. The centroid comes within 5 units of the source at
$t$ = `{python} f1(reach1)`. From then on the gradient is small and changes direction fast: the robots' direction estimates
scatter (up to `{python} deg(derr1[late1].max())` off), and the centroid stays within
`{python} f1(dist1[late1].max())` of the source, as Problem 1 asks. Note that the paper's simulation uses
$\epsilon_x = 0.5 > \epsilon_\mu = 0.001$, the opposite of the ordering in Theorem 1. The ordering is a sufficient
condition of the proof, and here the formation controller keeps $x$ almost still, so the centroid estimator has little to
track.

**Robots that fail (Remark 6 of the corrected paper).** Theorem 1 keeps the graph fixed. When robot $k$ stops and leaves
the graph, the estimates of the survivors no longer sum to zero: $\sum_{i\ne k}\hat x_i = -\hat x_k$. By Lemma 3 (ii) they
then converge with a common offset $c = -\hat x_k/(N-1)$ that never decays, and so does $\hat\mu$, which biases every
robot's direction. The fix is local. The surviving neighbours of $k$ hold its last estimates, and they split them evenly
among themselves:
$$
\hat x_i \leftarrow \hat x_i + \frac{\hat x_k}{|\mathcal N_k|}, \qquad \hat \mu_i \leftarrow \hat \mu_i + \frac{\hat \mu_k}{|\mathcal N_k|},
\qquad i \in \mathcal N_k .
$$
The sum is zero again, so the analysis of Theorem 1 applies to the survivors from that moment on, as long as their graph
stays connected. The published version has no such step, and neither does the run of its Fig. 7 (@sec-checks, item 4;
the rerun with and without the fix is in @sec-running).

```{python}
#| echo: false
# ---------------------------------------------------------------- Step 7: unicycles (Lemma 1, Prop. 6, Theorem 2)
D3 = PAPER["sim3"]
F3 = paper_field("sim3")
N3 = len(D3["p0"])
def deform_run(kappa, T=30.0, dt=0.01, wmax=0.0):
    o = {"model": "uni", "est": "central", "speed": D3["speed"], "kf": 0.0, "ex": 1.0, "emu": 1.0, "kappa": kappa, "wmax": wmax}
    run = simulate(F3, D3["p0"], [], o, T, dt, 10, theta0=D3["theta0"])
    X0 = relative(run[0]["p"])
    worst = 0.0
    for f in run:
        X = relative(f["p"])
        worst = max(worst, max(norm([X[i][0] - X0[i][0], X[i][1] - X0[i][1]]) for i in range(N3)))
    c = centroid(run[-1]["p"])
    return worst, norm([c[0] - source(F3)[0], c[1] - source(F3)[1]])
lem1 = cached("lemma1", lambda: [(k,) + deform_run(k) for k in (1.0, 2.0, 4.0)])
bound1 = lambda k: D3["speed"] * (N3 - 1) / N3 * 2 * math.pi / k
```

# Step 7: robots that drive at constant speed (Section V, Theorem 2) {#sec-step7}

A unicycle cannot stop and cannot move sideways; it can only turn. Each robot turns its heading $\alpha_i$ toward the
direction to follow, $m_d$ (at angle $\alpha_d$), with a proportional law and no feed-forward (the robots cannot know how
fast $m_d$ turns, since the field is unknown). The paper analyses $m_d = L^1_\sigma/\|L^1_\sigma\|$ and treats the
difference with $L_\sigma$ as a bounded deviation; its simulation, like this page, follows $L_\sigma$ itself:
$$
\omega_i = -\kappa_\gamma\,\delta_i, \qquad \delta_i = \alpha_i - \alpha_d \ \ (\text{wrapped to } (-\pi, \pi]).
$$
(The published version's formula for $\delta_i$ has the opposite sign; @sec-checks, item 2.)

- **Lemma 1.** All robots see the same $\alpha_d$, so the heading differences $\alpha_i - \alpha_j$ decay like
  $e^{-\kappa_\gamma t}$, and the shape can only drift a bounded amount: $\|x_i(t) - x_i(0)\| \le \frac{N-1}{N}\frac{2\pi}{\kappa_\gamma}$
  (times the speed, which the paper sets to 1).
- **Lemma 2 and Proposition 6.** Away from the source ($\|\nabla\sigma(p_c)\| \ge \varepsilon$) the direction $m_d$ turns at
  a bounded rate, so a large enough gain keeps every $|\delta_i|$ below any angle $\gamma$ after a finite time.
- **Theorem 2.** For every $\epsilon > 0$ there is a gain $\kappa_\gamma$ such that the centroid gets within $\epsilon$ of the
  source and stays there. The proof keeps a buffer zone $\mathcal A$ (where the gradient is tiny and control is lost)
  inside the target ball $\mathcal B$: once in $\mathcal A$ the centroid may wander out, but it cannot leave $\mathcal B$
  before the headings are back under control. The robots end up circling the source.

**Lemma 1 in the paper's Fig. 8 setting** ($N$ = `{python} N3` robots at speed `{python} D3["speed"]`, the field held
still, `{python} 30` seconds, no limit on the turn rate). The largest drift $\max_{i,t}\|x_i(t) - x_i(0)\|$ and the bound
$v\frac{N-1}{N}\frac{2\pi}{\kappa_\gamma}$:

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
rows = ["| $\\kappa_\\gamma$ | largest drift | bound of Lemma 1 | centroid to source at $t = 30$ |", "|---|---|---|---|"]
for k, worst, dfin in lem1:
    rows.append(f"| {f1(k)} | {f2(worst)} | {f2(bound1(k))} | {f2(dfin)} |")
print("\n".join(rows))
```

The drift stays inside the bound, with room to spare, and a larger gain keeps the shape tighter.

# What differs from the published version {#sec-checks}

The page's checks (the reruns, the census and the tests below) found the following errors in the published version (IEEE
TAC; arXiv:2410.15921v3, which will not be updated). The corrected version that this page follows fixes them all. They
concern statements and simulation details, not the method: the architecture works in every run on this page. Where the
published version is quoted below, the corrected one is what the rest of the page states.

**1. Proposition 4 is false as published.** The published version bounds the change of $\lambda_{\min}(S)$ when robot $j$
is removed, *with the coordinates recentred and $D$ recomputed*, by $4/(N-1)$. Removing a robot that sits far from the rest
changes $D$ a lot, and with it the normalisation of $S$. Counterexample: $N-1$ robots on a unit circle and one more at
distance 30; remove the far one.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
rows = ["| $N$ | $\\lambda_{\\min}(S(x))$ | after removing the far robot | change | published bound $4/(N-1)$ | change with the original $D$ | corrected bound $N/(N-1)^2$ |",
        "|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|"]
for N, a, b, d, bd, fx, bf in cx4:
    rows.append(f"| {N} | {f4(a)} | {f4(b)} | {f3(d)} | {f3(bd)} | {e2(fx)} | {f3(bf)} |")
print("\n".join(rows))
```

The change stays near 0.5 whatever $N$ is, so the bound fails for every $N \ge 10$. The census of @sec-step2 finds
`{python} cen[5]` violations in `{python} cen[0]` random swarms, the worst by a factor `{python} f2(cen[6])`. The proof
(Appendix A) bounds $D^{(-j)}$ from *above*, $D^{(-j)} \le \frac{N}{N-1}D$, but dividing by $(D^{(-j)})^2$ needs a bound
from *below*. **Correction:** normalise both matrices by the original $D$. The appendix's identity
$A^{(-j)} = A - \frac{N}{N-1}x_jx_j^\top$ gives
$$
\frac{P(x) - P(x^{(-j)})}{D^2} = \frac{N\,x_jx_j^\top}{(N-1)^2D^2} - \frac{A}{N(N-1)D^2},
$$
a difference of two positive semidefinite matrices of norms at most $N/(N-1)^2$ and $1/(N-1)$, so its norm is at most
the larger, $N/(N-1)^2$. The census finds `{python} cen[7]` violations of this bound (worst ratio
`{python} f2(cen[8])`, so it is nearly tight). The corrected version also adds the counterexample as a remark, to show
that the original $D$ cannot be replaced by the new one.

**2. The heading error $\delta_i$ of Section V has the wrong sign.** The published version defines
$\delta_i = \operatorname{atan2}\big((Em_i)^\top m_d,\ m_i^\top m_d\big)$ with $E$ the rotation by $+\pi/2$. Since
$(Em_i)^\top m_d = \sin(\alpha_d - \alpha_i)$, this is $\alpha_d - \alpha_i$, while the next line uses
$\dot\delta_i = \omega_i - \omega_d$, which is the derivative of $\alpha_i - \alpha_d$. With the definition as written,
$\omega_i = -\kappa_\gamma\delta_i$ turns every robot *away* from $m_d$. The paper's code uses $\alpha_i - \alpha_d$, which is
right. Rerunning Fig. 8 with the sign as written, the centroid ends `{python} f1(d3bad[-1])` units from the source instead
of `{python} f1(d3[-1])`. **Correction:** $\delta_i = \operatorname{atan2}\big((Em_d)^\top m_i,\ m_d^\top m_i\big)$. Relatedly,
$\omega_d := \|\dot m_d\|$ should be the signed rate $\dot\alpha_d$ (so that $\dot m_d = \omega_d E m_d$), since the proofs
use it with both signs. The appendix's proof of Lemma 2 already uses the corrected
convention, $\delta_{ij} = \alpha_i - \alpha_j$.

**3. Central symmetry does not imply isotropy.** After Corollary 1 the published version says that "for centrally symmetric
deployments, $S(x) \propto I_m$". Four robots at $(\pm2, \pm1)$ are centrally symmetric and have
$S(x) = \mathrm{diag}$(`{python} f2(Srect[0])`, `{python} f2(Srect[2])`), with $S_{12}$ = `{python} f2(Srect[1])`. Corollary 1 itself ($L_\sigma = L^1_\sigma$ in a quadratic field) is right; only the
step to "$L^1_\sigma$ is parallel to the gradient" needs isotropy as an extra assumption, which the corrected version
states.

**4. A robot that drops out leaves a permanent offset in the estimators, and the published version has no remedy.** Lemma 3 rests on the average of the estimates
being constant ($\hat y_c(t) = \hat y_c(0) = 0$). When robot $k$ stops and leaves the graph, the live robots keep
$\sum_{i \ne k}\hat x_i = -\hat x_k \ne 0$, so by Lemma 3 (ii) all their estimates converge to $x_i + c$ with the same
offset $c = -\hat x_k/(N-1)$; the same happens to $\hat\mu$. Every robot then places the centroid off by $c$, and the
direction estimate $\mu^i_c$ picks up a bias that does not decay (the offset $c$ weighted by the readings, plus the
same effect in $\hat\mu$). The more robots drop out at once, the larger it is. In the rerun of Fig. 7, at
$t = 10$ (`{python} int(na10)` robots left), the estimates are offset by $\|c\|$ = `{python} f3(norm(off10))`, the same for
every robot. During the approach ($1 \le t \le 15$) the worst direction error is `{python} deg(derr2[appr2].max())` with
dropouts, against `{python} deg(derr1[appr1].max())` in Fig. 6 without them. The paper's own logs show the same:
`{python} deg(log2[lapp2, 3].max())` in Fig. 7 against `{python} deg(log1[lapp1, 3].max())` in Fig. 6. The swarm still
reaches the source in both, so this is a matter of the theory's scope: Theorem 1 does not cover dropouts, while the
simulation of Fig. 7 is presented as evidence of resilience. **Correction** (Remark 6 of the corrected version, and
@sec-step6): the surviving neighbours of the failed robot split its last estimates among themselves, which restores the
zero sum with no global action. Rerun with this step, Fig. 7's offset at $t = 10$ is `{python} e2(norm(off10f))`
instead of `{python} f3(norm(off10))`. For $1 \le t \le 12$, before either run reaches the source, the worst robot's direction
error averages `{python} deg(derr2f[far2f].mean())` instead of `{python} deg(derr2[far2].mean())`, with brief peaks of
`{python} deg(derr2f[far2f].max())` just after a failure instead of `{python} deg(derr2[far2].max())`; and the centroid first comes within 5
units of the source at $t$ = `{python} f1(reach2f)` instead of `{python} f1(reach2)`. (Resetting every robot's estimates
to zero also restores the zero sum, but it needs every robot to act at once.)

**5. The signal of the simulations is printed differently from the one simulated.** Equation (22) of the published
version gives
$$
\text{“}\sigma(p) = k\frac{x_\sigma}{\|x_\sigma\|} - Q_a(x_\sigma - a)e^{\cdots} - Q_b(x_\sigma - b)e^{\cdots}\text{”},
$$
which is a vector:
up to signs and factors it is the gradient expression of the code. Its $Q_a = 0.9\left[\begin{smallmatrix}1/\sqrt{30} & 0\\ 1 & 0\end{smallmatrix}\right]$
has an entry out of place and the wrong sign: the code has $Q_a = -0.9\,\mathrm{diag}(1/\sqrt{30}, 1)$. The field the code
simulates is the one in @sec-problem. Also, $p_\sigma = (40, 40)$ is the centre $c$ of the formula, not the maximum: the
maximum is at (`{python} f2(S1[0])`, `{python} f2(S1[1])`) for Fig. 6, and at (`{python} f2(S2[0])`, `{python} f2(S2[1])`)
rather than $(35, -35)$ for Fig. 7. Finally, the term $-k\|X\|$ makes this field a cone at $c$, so it is not $C^2$ there
and its Hessian is unbounded, against Definition 2. This is harmless for the robots (they only read values), and $c$ is
`{python} f1(cone_dist)` units from the source in Fig. 6. **Correction:** the corrected version prints the field of
@sec-problem, calls its centre $c_\sigma$, gives the true maxima, and notes the cone.

**6. Smaller things,** all corrected:

- The ten-robot graph of Figs. 4 and 5 has algebraic connectivity `{python} f3(lam2_10)`, not 0.26.
- Fig. 6: the text says 20 robots, the caption says 30; the log has `{python} N1`.
- The simulations use $\epsilon_x = 0.5$ and $\epsilon_\mu = 0.001$, so the direction estimator is 500 times faster than the
  centroid estimator, the opposite of the ordering $\epsilon_x < \epsilon_\mu$ of Theorem 1 and of the second assumption
  of Section IV-E. It works because the formation controller keeps $x$ almost constant, so the centroid estimator has
  little to track (as the paper remarks).
- Equation (15) has $(p^i_d - x^j_d)$ where $(p^i_d - p^j_d)$ is meant.
- Fig. 8 is run with $L_\sigma$ computed centrally (as the conclusion says), at speed 12, with $\kappa_\gamma = 1$ and the
  turn rate clipped to $|\omega_i| \le 1.5$. The analysis of Section V has unit speed and no clipping, and Theorem 2 asks
  for a large enough gain. The simulation works anyway; this page uses the same settings for its rerun.

# The program each robot runs {#sec-program}

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}
**Before take-off:** the gains $v$, $k_f$, $\epsilon_x$, $\epsilon_\mu$ (and $\kappa_\gamma$ for a unicycle), its desired
offsets $p^d_i - p^d_j$ to its neighbours, and $\hat x_i = \hat\mu_i = 0$.

**At every tick:** read $\sigma(p_i)$; measure $p_i - p_j$ for every neighbour; receive $\hat x_j$, $\mu_j$, $\hat\mu_j$.
Then:

1. $\mu_i = \sigma(p_i)\,\hat x_i$ and $\mu^i_c = \mu_i - \hat\mu_i$ (its estimate of the climbing direction).
2. Point robot: velocity $v\,\mu^i_c/\|\mu^i_c\| - k_f\sum_j[(p_i - p_j) - (p^d_i - p^d_j)]$.
   Unicycle: turn rate $-\kappa_\gamma\,\mathrm{wrap}(\alpha_i - \arg\mu^i_c)$.
3. Update $\hat x_i$ and $\hat\mu_i$ by one Euler step of the two estimators, and send $\hat x_i$, $\mu_i$, $\hat\mu_i$ to
   the neighbours.

**When a neighbour $k$ falls silent** (Remark 6 of the corrected paper): drop it from the neighbour list, and add
$\hat x_k/|\mathcal N_k|$ and $\hat\mu_k/|\mathcal N_k|$, its last estimates divided by its number of surviving
neighbours, to $\hat x_i$ and $\hat\mu_i$ (`core.fail`). This needs each robot to know how many live neighbours $k$
had, which $k$ can send along with its estimates.
:::

The same, as a function of what robot $i$ has at one tick (`core.step` runs it for every robot, with the same arithmetic):

```{python}
#| code-fold: false
def program(sig, xh, muh, rel, nbr, des, o, dt):
    """Robot i. sig = sigma(p_i); xh, muh = its estimates; rel[j] = p_i - p_j (measured);
    nbr[j] = (xh_j, mu_j, muh_j) (received); des[j] = p^d_i - p^d_j. Returns (velocity, new xh, new muh)."""
    mu = [sig * xh[0], sig * xh[1]]
    muc = [mu[0] - muh[0], mu[1] - muh[1]]
    n = math.hypot(muc[0], muc[1])
    u = [o["speed"] * muc[0] / n, o["speed"] * muc[1] / n] if n > 0 else [0.0, 0.0]
    dx, dm = [0.0, 0.0], [0.0, 0.0]
    for j, (xhj, muj, muhj) in nbr.items():
        for k in (0, 1):
            dx[k] -= (xh[k] - xhj[k]) - rel[j][k]
            dm[k] -= (muh[k] - muhj[k]) - (mu[k] - muj[k])
            u[k] -= o["kf"] * (rel[j][k] - des[j][k])
    new_xh = [xh[k] + dt / o["ex"] * dx[k] for k in (0, 1)]
    new_muh = [muh[k] + dt / o["emu"] * dm[k] for k in (0, 1)]
    return u, new_xh, new_muh
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
# the function above gives the same tick as core.step, robot by robot
W = world(P1)
W["xh"] = [[0.3 * q[0], 0.2 * q[1]] for q in X1]
W["muh"] = [[0.01 * q[1], -0.02 * q[0]] for q in X1]
o1 = {"model": "si", "est": "dist", "speed": 10.0, "kf": 0.1, "ex": 0.5, "emu": 0.001}
nb = {i: {} for i in range(N1)}
for i, j in E1:
    nb[i][j] = j
    nb[j][i] = i
mus = [[sigma(F1, W["p"][i]) * W["xh"][i][0], sigma(F1, W["p"][i]) * W["xh"][i][1]] for i in range(N1)]
mine = []
for i in range(N1):
    rel = {j: [W["p"][i][0] - W["p"][j][0], W["p"][i][1] - W["p"][j][1]] for j in nb[i]}
    des = {j: [W["Pd"][i][0] - W["Pd"][j][0], W["Pd"][i][1] - W["Pd"][j][1]] for j in nb[i]}
    nbr = {j: (W["xh"][j], mus[j], W["muh"][j]) for j in nb[i]}
    u, xh, muh = program(sigma(F1, W["p"][i]), W["xh"][i], W["muh"][i], rel, nbr, des, o1, 1e-4)
    mine.append([W["p"][i][0] + 1e-4 * u[0], W["p"][i][1] + 1e-4 * u[1]] + xh + muh)
step(F1, W, E1, o1, 1e-4)
diff_prog = max(abs(a - b) for i in range(N1) for a, b in zip(mine[i], W["p"][i] + W["xh"][i] + W["muh"][i]))
```

Run robot by robot on the example's twenty robots (with nonzero estimates), it gives the same tick as `core.step` (largest difference
`{python} e2(diff_prog)`).

```{python}
        a.scatter([q[0] for q, ok in zip(f["p"], f["alive"]) if not ok], [q[1] for q, ok in zip(f["p"], f["alive"]) if not ok], s=9, color=RED, zorder=5)

        if k == 2:

        b.set_ylabel(lab, fontsize=8.5); b.grid(alpha=0.25)
        if k < 2:
            b.set_xticklabels([])
    b.set_xlabel("t")
    plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
fig_si(r1, F1, T1, dist1, cerr1, derr1, log1, (-55, 75), (-60, 65), "Fig. 6: 20 robots")
def logdiff(run, log, tmax=15.0):
    worst = 0.0
    for row in log:
        if row[0] > tmax:
            break
        f = min(run, key=lambda f: abs(f["t"] - row[0]))
        c = centroid([q for q, ok in zip(f["p"], f["alive"]) if ok])
        worst = max(worst, norm([c[0] - row[1], c[1] - row[2]]))
    return worst
ld1, ld2 = logdiff(r1, log1), logdiff(r2, log2)
reach2 = float(T2[np.argmax(dist2 < 5)])
```

# What changes with more robots, and what this page does not cover {#sec-limits}

- **More robots** make the swarm *resilient* in the sense of Proposition 4: one robot more or less changes $\lambda_{\min}$
  by about $1/N$ of the original $D^2$ **[proved]**.
  The estimators slow down when the graph gets sparse ($\lambda_2$ shrinks), which costs communication rate, not
  correctness **[proved]** (Lemma 3).
- **Dropouts.** With the correction of Remark 6, the analysis of Theorem 1 starts again after each failure, as long as
  the survivors stay connected **[proved]**. Failures that come faster than the estimators converge, and graphs that
  split, are not covered **[open]**; without the correction, the swarm still reached the source in every run of this
  page **[numerical]**.
- **The time scales.** Theorem 1 asks for small $\epsilon_x < \epsilon_\mu$ without a number. The playground lets you slow
  the estimators down until the swarm gets lost **[numerical]**.
- **Unicycles with the distributed estimators.** The paper's unicycle results (Section V) assume $m_d$ is known exactly,
  and its Fig. 8 computes $L_\sigma$ centrally. The playground's first simulator runs unicycles with the two estimators of
  Section IV; it works, but this is **[numerical]** (the paper's last remark says the bounds get more conservative).
- **Not simulated here:** three dimensions ($m = 3$, covered by Sections II to IV), noise in the readings or in the
  measured positions, communication delays, and graphs that change with distance.
- **Assumptions every example keeps:** a fixed connected graph, a common orientation for the relative positions, exact
  readings, and one maximum.

# Glossary {#sec-glossary}

| symbol | meaning |
|---|---|
| $N$, $p_i$, $p_c$ | number of robots, position of robot $i$, centroid $\frac1N\sum_i p_i$ |
| $x_i = p_i - p_c$, $D$ | the deployment (positions around the centroid) and its size $\max_i\|x_i\|$ |
| $P(x)$, $S(x)$ | second-moment matrix $\frac1N\sum_i x_ix_i^\top$, and $S = P/D^2$ |
| $\sigma$, $p_\sigma$ | the signal and its maximum (the source) |
| $K$, $M$ | bounds $\|\nabla\sigma\| \le K$, $\|H_\sigma\| \le 2M$; $K^{\min}_{\mathcal S}$, $M_{\mathcal S}$ on a set $\mathcal S$ |
| $L_\sigma$, $L^1_\sigma$, $R$ | the robots' direction $\frac{1}{ND^2}\sum_i\sigma(p_i)x_i$, its always-ascending part $S\nabla\sigma$, the remainder |
| $D^{\max}_{\mathcal S}$ | $\frac{K^{\min}_{\mathcal S}}{M_{\mathcal S}}\lambda_{\min}(S)$, the size below which $L_\sigma$ climbs (Prop. 2) |
| $\mathcal G$, $L$, $\lambda_2$ | the graph, its Laplacian, its algebraic connectivity |
| $\hat x_i$ | robot $i$'s estimate of $x_i$ (so $p_i - \hat x_i$ is where it puts the centroid) |
| $\mu_i$, $\mu_c$, $\hat\mu_i$, $\mu^i_c$ | $\sigma(p_i)\hat x_i$, their average, robot $i$'s estimate of $\mu_i - \mu_c$, its direction $\mu_i - \hat\mu_i$ |
| $\epsilon_x$, $\epsilon_\mu$ | time scales of the two estimators (smaller is faster) |
| $v$, $k_f$, $p^d$ | speed, formation gain, desired shape |
| $\alpha_i$, $\alpha_d$, $\delta_i$, $\kappa_\gamma$ | unicycle heading, heading to follow, heading error $\alpha_i - \alpha_d$, turning gain |
